blocks.content: Picture a highway that narrows from six lanes down to one for about a mile, then opens back up to six lanes again. It does not matter how wide the rest of the highway is. Every single car has to squeeze through that one lane, so that one lane decides how fast traffic moves overall.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396381538-843860116.png
blocks.alt: A request passes through four steps, one slow step caps how fast the whole chain can go

blocks.content: That narrow stretch of highway is the origin of the word bottleneck, and the idea maps onto software almost perfectly. In a system design interview, this is one of the most reliable ways to tell a candidate who assembled familiar boxes from one who actually understands what they drew.
1. Introduction

A bottleneck is the single component that limits how fast or how much your whole system can handle, no matter how much you scale everything else around it. You can double the app servers, triple the cache size, and add five more edge locations, and none of it matters if the one constrained piece stays exactly as constrained as before.

This is not a niche concept you pull out for one specific question. It is a lens you apply to every design you draw. Once you have boxes and arrows on the whiteboard, the very next useful question is always the same one: which one of these boxes breaks first.
1.1 The one slow part rule

Say you put ten app server instances behind a load balancer, all stateless, all scaled beautifully, and all of them talk to one single database instance. It feels like a solid, scaled system. It is not. Every one of those ten instances is funneling requests into the same database, so the system as a whole runs at the speed of that one database, not at the combined speed of ten servers.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A bottleneck is not always the part of the diagram that looks the most complicated. Often it is the plainest box on the page, a single instance you forgot to scale, a single lock, a single sequential step that everything else has to wait behind.
2. Why Interviewers Care About This

Nearly anyone who has read a few system design articles can draw a load balancer, a stateless service tier, a cache, and a database, and arrange them into something that looks correct. That drawing on its own does not tell an interviewer much. What tells them something is whether you, unprompted, point at your own diagram and say here is the piece that gives out first.
A candidate who says here is where this breaks first is showing they understand the system, not just that they can assemble one.

Interviewers often deliberately do not ask what is the bottleneck here. They wait to see whether it comes up on its own. Staying quiet about it is not neutral, it reads as either not having thought about it or not knowing how to spot it, and both are worse than naming a bottleneck that turns out to be only partly right.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: Even a slightly wrong guess at the bottleneck, defended with real reasoning, lands better than silence. The reasoning is what is actually being graded.
3. Common Bottleneck Patterns

Most systems strain in one of a small number of predictable shapes. You will not spot every bottleneck by memorizing a checklist, but learning to recognize these five shapes gets you most of the way there, in interviews and in systems you actually operate.

["A single database instance taking heavy write load while everything around it is scaled out.","A single service instance that was never given horizontal scaling, sitting among services that were.","A synchronous call chain where the slowest downstream service caps the latency of the entire request.","A shared resource, a lock or a rate limited third party API, that every request has to pass through one at a time.","A hot partition or hot key, where load is wildly uneven across a system that is otherwise scaled out fine."]
items: A single database instance taking heavy write load while everything around it is scaled out.
A single service instance that was never given horizontal scaling, sitting among services that were.
A synchronous call chain where the slowest downstream service caps the latency of the entire request.
A shared resource, a lock or a rate limited third party API, that every request has to pass through one at a time.
A hot partition or hot key, where load is wildly uneven across a system that is otherwise scaled out fine.

blocks.content: 3.1 The single database under write load
blocks.text: 3.1 The single database under write load

blocks.content: This is the most common one, by a wide margin. Reads scale relatively easily, you can cache them, replicate them, spread them across replicas. Writes are harder, every write typically has to land on one primary at some point, so as write volume grows, that primary is doing more and more work while nothing else in the system changes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396381538-640291394.png
blocks.alt: Ten scaled app server instances all funnel their writes into one database instance

blocks.content: Adding more app servers here does nothing for the actual constraint. It just means more requests arriving at the same database at the same time, all waiting for their turn.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Scaling the layer that is easy to scale, usually the stateless app tier, while the actual constraint sits one layer down at the database, untouched.
3.2 The single service instance

Sometimes one service in an otherwise well scaled architecture just never got the horizontal scaling treatment. Maybe it holds some in memory state nobody wants to touch, maybe it was the last thing built and nobody circled back. Whatever the reason, that one instance becomes a hard ceiling on throughput for anything that depends on it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396381539-988238636.png
blocks.alt: A payment service running as a single instance next to other services that each run ten instances

blocks.content: 3.3 The synchronous call chain

A request comes in, calls service A, which waits for and calls service B, which waits for and calls service C. If C is slow, the whole chain is slow, even if A and B individually respond in a couple of milliseconds. The overall latency of a synchronous chain is roughly the sum of its parts, and it is always capped by the slowest link.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396381540-133632718.png
blocks.alt: A synchronous request chain where one slow inventory service delays the entire reply

blocks.content: This one is easy to miss because none of the individual services look broken in isolation. You only see it by tracing the full path a request takes end to end.
3.4 Shared resources: locks and rate limited APIs
blocks.text: 3.4 Shared resources: locks and rate limited APIs

blocks.content: Any resource that many requests share and can only use one at a time, or a limited number at a time, becomes a bottleneck the moment concurrency rises past what it can handle. A lock inside your own code is one version of this. A third party API with a hard rate limit is another, and it is arguably worse, because you cannot fix it by scaling your own infrastructure at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396381540-462572176.png
blocks.alt: Three concurrent requests all waiting on the same shared lock

blocks.title: Watch out for this
blocks.content: It is tempting to assume every dependency scales as generously as your own services do. Third party payment providers, SMS gateways, and external search APIs usually do not, and their limits become your bottleneck whether you designed for it or not.
3.5 Hot partitions and hot keys

You can shard a system beautifully across a hundred partitions and still get bitten by this one. If one key, one celebrity account, one viral product, one trending post, gets a wildly disproportionate share of the traffic, that single partition absorbs load nothing else in the system sees. The rest of your infrastructure can be sitting nearly idle while one partition is on fire.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396381541-956024841.png
blocks.alt: One celebrity user drives all their traffic to a single partition while everyone else spreads evenly across the rest

blocks.content: 4. The Technique: What Breaks First

Here is a habit that separates strong candidates from average ones. After you sketch your design, before the interviewer even asks a follow up question, walk through it yourself and ask out loud, as load goes up, what breaks first.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396381541-992958127.png
blocks.alt: A candidate sketches a design, then deliberately asks what breaks first as load increases

blocks.content: Doing this proactively is a strong signal on its own. It shows you are not just presenting a finished artifact, you are actively stress testing your own thinking in front of the interviewer.
4.1 Walking your own design
A simple way to do this systematically is to trace the path of a single request through your diagram, component by component, and ask a short set of questions at each stop.

["Can this component scale horizontally, and if not, is that a problem at the traffic level we are designing for.","Is this call synchronous or asynchronous, and if synchronous, how slow is the slowest thing downstream of it.","Does this step touch any shared resource, a lock, a queue, a rate limited external API, that everything else has to funnel through.","Is load actually spread evenly here, or could one key, one user, one partition absorb far more than its share."]
items: Can this component scale horizontally, and if not, is that a problem at the traffic level we are designing for.
Is this call synchronous or asynchronous, and if synchronous, how slow is the slowest thing downstream of it.
Does this step touch any shared resource, a lock, a queue, a rate limited external API, that everything else has to funnel through.
Is load actually spread evenly here, or could one key, one user, one partition absorb far more than its share.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: Do not just say the database might be a bottleneck as a throwaway line. Say why, and say what would actually happen, writes queueing up, timeouts appearing downstream, whatever the concrete symptom would be.
5. Matching Fixes to Bottleneck Type
Naming a bottleneck is only half the job. The fix you propose next should follow logically from the kind of bottleneck it is, not just be a reflex answer like add a cache to everything.
5.1 Database write bottlenecks

If writes are the constraint, sharding spreads writes across multiple primaries by key. Read replicas help enormously if the workload is read heavy, since they take load off the primary entirely for anything that does not need to be perfectly fresh. Caching helps for hot read paths. None of these three directly solve a pure write throughput problem the way sharding does, so pick based on what is actually saturating.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396381542-930538522.png
blocks.alt: A single primary database gains two read replicas so reads no longer compete with writes

blocks.content: 5.2 Compute bottlenecks

When the constraint is CPU or memory on a stateless service, horizontal scaling behind a load balancer is the standard answer. The word stateless matters here, if the service is quietly holding session state or in memory data that a request depends on, adding instances just introduces a new problem of routing the right requests to the right instance.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396381542-629601919.png
blocks.alt: A single service instance becomes three instances behind a load balancer

blocks.content: 5.3 Hot key bottlenecks

More partitions do not fix a hot key, since the hot key just sits on one of the new partitions and stays exactly as hot. What actually helps is changing the partition key itself so that no single key can dominate a shard, or coalescing repeated requests for the same hot data into one shared lookup instead of letting a thousand identical requests all hit the same partition independently.
6. Every Fix Creates a New Bottleneck
blocks.text: 6. Every Fix Creates a New Bottleneck

blocks.content: Nothing here is free. Every fix you propose removes one constraint and, almost always, introduces a different one somewhere else. Naming that new constraint, without being asked, is the kind of thing that reads as senior level thinking in an interview.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382286-771306341.png
blocks.alt: A database bottleneck gets fixed with a cache, which introduces cache invalidation complexity

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bottleneck type","Typical fix","New bottleneck it introduces"],"rows":[["Database write load","Sharding or write batching","Cross shard queries get harder, resharding later is painful"],["Read heavy database","Read replicas","Replication lag, replicas can serve slightly stale data"],["Slow or repeated reads","Add a cache","Cache invalidation, stale data if invalidation is wrong"],["Single service instance","Horizontal scaling","Need to externalize state, sticky routing gets more complex"],["Hot key or hot partition","Better partition key or coalescing","More complex routing logic, coalescing adds latency for individual callers"]]}

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: You are not looking for a design with zero bottlenecks. That does not exist. You are looking for the current bottleneck to move somewhere less painful, and for you to know where it moved to.
7. Worked Example: Photo Sharing App
Take a simple photo sharing app. Users upload photos, other users view a feed of recent photos. One app server tier, one database. Nothing exotic yet.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382289-364232686.png
blocks.alt: A photo sharing app with a mobile client, one app server, and one database

blocks.content: 7.1 First bottleneck: the database

As the user base grows, both uploads and feed reads land on the same single database instance. Uploads are writes, feed views are reads, and they are now competing for the same connections, the same disk, the same everything.

blocks.title: Doing the numbers
blocks.text: Say the app now handles 500 requests per second, split roughly between uploads and feed reads. The single database instance realistically tops out around 200 requests per second before latency climbs sharply. The other 300 requests per second either queue up behind it or start timing out.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Reaching for more app server instances first, because that is the easy scaling lever, when the actual constraint here is one layer down at the database.
7.2 The fix: read replicas

Feed reads are the larger share of traffic here, and they do not need perfectly fresh data, a few seconds of staleness on a feed is unnoticeable. So read replicas are a strong fit, route feed reads to replicas, keep uploads going straight to the primary. The primary is now doing far less work overall, since it only handles writes and whatever reads truly need to be fresh.
7.3 The next bottleneck surfaces

Uploads keep growing on their own, independent of feed traffic, and they still all land on one primary. At the same time, the app server is doing image resizing synchronously as part of handling each upload request, and that CPU heavy work starts to dominate its own capacity before the database even becomes the constraint again.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396382289-106622161.png
blocks.alt: After read replicas are added, the app server CPU handling image resizing becomes the next bottleneck

blocks.content: The obvious next fix is moving image resizing off the request path entirely, into a background worker queue. That helps immediately, but now the queue depth and the number of workers processing it become the thing to watch, and if uploads spike faster than workers can drain the queue, users start seeing their photos take longer and longer to appear. The cycle from section six is still running, it just moved.
8. The Interview Angle

Bottleneck identification is usually the moment an interview shifts gears. Up to this point, the conversation has mostly been about whether you can produce a design at all, boxes, arrows, the right technologies in the right places. From here on, it becomes about whether you actually understand what you built.
Anyone can draw the boxes. Naming the one that breaks first, unprompted, is what shows you understand the system.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: Do not wait for the interviewer to ask what is the bottleneck here. By the time they ask, you want to already be a few steps ahead, explaining what you would do about it and what that fix would cost you.

Practice this on every design you sketch, even outside of interviews. Sketch it, then ask what breaks first as load increases, then ask what your fix would break next. That loop, repeated a few times, is most of what bottleneck identification actually is.
